sections.text: ये हि संस्पर्शजा भोगा दुःखयोनय एव ते।
The joys that spring from external associations bring pain; they have their beginning and their endings. The wise man does not rejoice in them.
He who, before he leaves his body, learns to surmount the promptings of desire and anger is a saint and is happy.
He who is happy within his Self and has found Its peace, and in whom the inner light shines, that sage attains Eternal Bliss and becomes the Spirit Itself.

We are discussing chapter 5, Sannyasa Yoga, Yoga of Renunciation. Renunciation is always about anything that we think we are possessing -- in this case, our actions. We think our actions are our own, and therefore renouncing those actions is the renunciation. So far we have learnt in Bhagavad Gita who we are as limited beings. As we had discussed many times before, the first six chapters of Bhagavad Gita describe tvam in that Mahavakya Tat Tvam Asi -- That Thou Art. Thou, the you, is what we have learned so far. In chapter one, we encountered the situation which we encounter in our daily life.
A common man facing day-to-day situations which never come clean-cut as black and white, good or bad, happy or unhappy. They always have complexity which makes me confused about what is right and wrong, which action to take. So we have seen Arjunas situation. He cannot see whether there is good in fighting the battle or running away from it. Fighting the battle is going to create some collateral damage, as we have seen recently in Afghanistan. Some people who I really respect and revere may also get hurt or killed.
And that happens in our life all the time. So the first chapter describes our situation as we face it in life today. The second chapter told us that what we think we are is not who we are. So there is a paradigm shift for us. We consider this self to be this limited me -- this body, mind, and intellect. And at the end of my journey in this life, this self will be destroyed.
But the self that I truly am will never be destroyed. Death will be only for the body. So thats a paradigm shift for us. Now, understanding that still does not give me what to do next. So the third chapter gave us the instruction about how to work in this world in an efficient manner. Two things it told us.
One, it says Swadharma Nidhanam Shreya, Paradharma Bhayavah. Act according to your own nature, your own Prakriti, because thats where your welfare is. Your good is in acting according to your nature. Paradharma Bhayavah -- others Dharma may seem very noble, very excellent, but you cannot follow that because thats not your Dharma. Act according to your Dharma, and act for the greater good -- not just in a selfish manner for your own good, but in a way that helps the greater community. We called it Karma Yoga.
The art of acting in this world in a way that purifies my mind and intellect is called Karma Yoga. Then chapter four says, once you have learned how to act outside in this world, now you have to renounce these actions which you consider yours. Even while Im practicing Karma Yoga, I still think Im practicing Karma Yoga. So there is still agency involved -- I am doing it. The fourth chapter says you have to now renounce these actions in knowledge -- knowledge which you already learned in chapter two.
That is, the self which I consider the self is not the real self. What I consider the self is actually the equipment belonging to the self -- body, mind, and intellect. So in chapter four it says: learn this knowledge about the self and renounce these actions, understanding that these actions belong to the Prakriti, to this body, mind, and intellect -- they do not belong to me, the self. Thats chapter four.
Chapter five -- we started seeing Karma Sannyasa. Now, how to really gain this Sannyasa which we talked about in chapter four?
So we have this detailed instruction about how to think, how to adjust our attitude towards actions. And the first thing it said is, think that you are not doing anything. And then it says, Brahmani Yadhaya, Karmani, Sangam, Tyaktva Karutiyah. The person who devote all his actions to the Brahman, that universal self, not just myself as the limited self, but I am doing it for that greater self. Then he does not incur any sin. He does not incur any negative impression on his mind.
Our problem is we take our actions so personally that somebody says, Rajan, you are not doing well. We get hurt right away. Right away it tells me that this person is not respecting me and it starts putting the negative impression. So the next time when I have to do that, Ill be thinking twice, should I be doing it? Will people appreciate it or will it not be appreciated? So that negative impression will not be on the mind of a person who is not doing it with this limited ego.
Because to him, action is an action, the result is a result. So he has no impression on his mind. So such a person will act in this world like a Padmapatra, the lotus leaf which remaining in the water coming out of the mud does not ever get tainted by any of that. Water falls on it, it rolls off. So thats the technique given to us in this chapter. In such a person who is constantly thinking about his self as the greater self will be liberated from these limitations.
And then we have seen: how will such a Yogi behave in this world once he gets to that level? Bahyasparseshu Asaktatma -- he is unattached to the contacts outside. Sa Brahma Yoga Yuktamatma Sukham Akshayam Ashnute -- we are constantly seeking unlimited happiness. We are not seeking limited happiness, though we think we are happy if we get some limited happiness.
Green card, Green card, Green card. Once I have it I wont ask for anything more. But I know the next thing Ill ask is -- now I got the green card, maybe I need to find the right person to get married. So people say take a vacation for three weeks from your job, go to India to find a bride. And they say, Rajan, I cant do it in three weeks because my parents have lined up so many girls to meet.
But I think I still need some more time. Can I get two more weeks of vacation? And then it continues. We are seeking unlimited happiness. And Bhagavan said theres only one formula that works. Sua Saktatma is unattached to the context outside in this world.
Sa Brahma Yogi Yuktatma -- such a person is a Yogi. He is one with the Brahman, connected with the Brahman. And all of this seems very difficult to practice. So the next verse says, remember -- what is there if I am going to avoid all these pleasures in my life? What is the fun of living life?
When I was a teenager, we used to have this joke: when you go up to Chitragupta, he will ask what you did with your life. So we have to justify -- if you didnt experience anything, what did you do? Go back, experience all that, and then come back. So we think, if I dont experience any pleasure in this world, what is there to live this life for? They say, well, you can experience all these pleasures.
Remember, Ye hi samsparshaja bhoga dukha yonaya -- these pleasures coming out of contact with the objects in the world outside have a limited capacity; they are actually a womb of unhappiness. So unless you are careful, you will realize that these pleasures are Adi and Antavanta -- they start at one point in time and will end. So you dont get Ramate, dont get engrossed in them. You experience the pleasure and move on.
Its not that its a nice day, Im saying no, I mean this is not good. I mean how can you have a nice day? How can I enjoy nice day? Gita tells me its all Adiyanta Vanta. But when theres a nice day, enjoy it. But next day when theres not nice, dont complain.
Thats all it says -- not that you are going to complain about why we dont have nice days, why hes not controlling the climate. We know this is the reality of life. The next three verses tell us why one should be detached from these contacts outside, and how. Shaknoteehaiva yaha sodhum prak shareera vimokshanaat, Kama krodh udbhavam vegam, sa yuktaha sa sukhi naraha.
The happy person definition is here. We are very happy, elated. I read on Facebook somewhere that may your life be as happy as it seems on Facebook. Because we know that thats not the reality, right? We are not putting all the garbage from our life on the Facebook. So Sukhi who is truly sukhi, not who appears to be happy.
We all appear to be happy from the other persons point of view. Rajan, youre doing very well. Only Rajan knows how he is doing, right? Bhagavan said, Shaknoti hi evaha yaha sodhum prak shareera vimokshanath -- before this body disintegrates, who can withhold the vega, the power, the udbhavam, that force which is generated in my mind by Kama (desire) and Krodha (anger)?
It did not say you will not have Kama or Krodha. Vega is the operative word here. When it is flowing peacefully in a serene manner, it is the most enjoyable thing, right? People enjoy the river. Some of our friends have houses right on the river. And we all go in envy and say James river.
When a storm was predicted, people were preparing. But the James River, when it is flowing peacefully, there is no problem. It gives peace and happiness to anybody. Our mind is like the river. When it is flowing in a peaceful, serene manner, it takes you towards happiness. When do we think about inspired projects or inspired actions? When we feel happy. When we are calm and happy, then we say, lets do this.
When I am upset, no matter how good an idea is put in front of me, forget about it. So the mind has to be serene and flowing in an appropriate manner towards its goal. Then only can peace and happiness come. But when this uninvited guest -- the flood -- comes, it will be manifold, uncontrollable, and anything that comes in its way will be destroyed. Bhagavan said that Kama and Krodha, when that desire is so powerful that you are rushing towards the object of desire and whatever comes in your way you want to destroy --
Thats anger. That Vega should be withheld. A person who can withhold the force of Kama and Krodha in his mind is Yukta -- he is the one who is connected with his own self. He will then be happy in all situations, because he has control over the flow of his thoughts. Mind, as we have learned in Tattva Bodhi, is nothing but the flow of thoughts.
One thought does not make a mind. The second thought creates the genesis of mind. Then more and more thoughts -- the second thought gives rise to the third, the fourth, and the fifth in the same direction. Thoughts flowing in one direction create a focused mind. As long as the mind is flowing toward the right destination in a disciplined manner, it creates happiness. When my desires are all over the place -- I want to be a billionaire, and then I also want to become a wise person, and then I also want to be a sports personality -- then Im torn all over and creating disaster.
A person who develops this capacity before this body disintegrates -- because after that you dont really have any chance -- this is your chance to create discipline in your mind. Such a person is Sukhi Naraha. The verse says Yo Antaha Sukho -- one who finds happiness within.

Verse 22 delivers a sobering truth about worldly pleasures: The joys that spring from external associations bring pain; they have their beginning and their endings. This is not pessimism but precise observation - every contact-born pleasure is inherently temporary, carrying within it the seed of its own ending. Verse 23 then offers the practical challenge: master the promptings of desire and anger before death. Verse 24 reveals the reward: one who is happy within his Self and in whom the inner light shines attains Eternal Bliss and becomes the Spirit Itself.
Today, observe the adi-antavanta (beginning-and-ending) nature of pleasures. When you enjoy your morning coffee, notice it begins, peaks, and ends. When a pleasant conversation lifts your mood, watch how the feeling fades. This is not to become joyless but to see clearly - as verse 22 says, the wise man does not rejoice in them because he knows their nature. The more profound practice from verse 23 is working with kama (desire) and krodha (anger). Notice that the verse says to surmount their promptings - not eliminate desire and anger, but master their vega (force). When desire arises today, can you feel its pull without being swept away? When anger flares, can you experience its heat without acting from it? This mastery, Krishna promises, leads to the state of verse 24: antah-sukha (inner happiness), antar-arama (inner rejoicing), and antar-jyoti (inner light). Even a glimpse of this inner fullness changes everything.
